entries.meaning: He reverently bowed his head at my feet and then related his doubt. Hearing his humble, gentle words, I lovingly told him, Bhavani: ‘Garuda, you have met me along the road; how can I properly explain this to you? All your doubts will be broken only when you keep holy company for a long time. There you should hear the lovely story of Hari, sung in many ways by sages, in which Lord Rama is the divine subject at beginning, middle and end. Brother, I shall send you where Hari's story is told continually; go there and hear it. As you listen, every doubt will depart and immense love for Rama's feet will arise.’

‘Raghupati is not attained without love, even through yoga, austerity, knowledge and dispassion. To the north is a lovely blue mountain where virtuous Kaka Bhushundi lives. Supremely skilled in devotion's path, learned, a home of virtues and ancient, he tells Rama's story without cease, while many fine birds listen reverently. Go there and hear Hari's abundant virtues; the sorrow born of delusion will go far away.’ When I had explained everything, he bowed at my feet and joyfully departed. That is why, Uma, I did not explain it myself; through Raghupati's grace I understood the secret. Perhaps he had once conceived pride, and the treasure of grace wished to remove it. Moreover, I concealed nothing from him—a bird best understands the language of another bird. The Lord's Maya is powerful, Bhavani; what wise person is there whom it has not deluded?

Garuda reached the place where Bhushundi lives, his understanding unobstructed and devotion to Hari unbroken. At the sight of the mountain his mind grew serene; Maya, delusion and sorrow all departed. After bathing and drinking in the lake, he went delighted beneath the banyan. Very aged birds had gathered there to hear Rama's lovely deeds. Just as Bhushundi was about to begin the story, the lord of birds arrived. Seeing the king of birds approach, the crow and the whole gathering rejoiced. He honoured Garuda greatly, asked after his welfare and gave him a fine seat. After worshipping him with love, the crow spoke sweet words.

Garuda said, ‘Listen, dear one: everything for which I came has happened simply by receiving your sight. At the sight of your supremely holy hermitage, delusion, doubt and manifold error have gone. Now, dear one, reverently tell me the most purifying story of Shri Rama, eternally delightful and destroyer of masses of pain. Again and again, master, I humbly entreat you.’ Hearing Garuda's humble, candid, deeply loving, joyful and holy speech, the crow's heart filled with supreme enthusiasm and he began to tell the profound account of Raghupati's virtues. First, Bhavani, with deep love he described the lake of Rama's deeds; then he told of Narada's vast delusion and, later, of Ravana's incarnation. He next sang the story of the Lord's descent and attentively told his childhood deeds.

He next told of Rama's impending consecration and how the king's promise broke the joy of kingship; the citizens' grief of separation and the dialogue between Rama and Lakshmana; the forest departure, the boatman's devotion, the crossing of the Ganga and residence at Prayaga; the Lord's meeting with Valmiki and how the Lord dwelt at Chitrakuta. He spoke much of the minister's return, the king's death, Bharata's arrival and love; of Bharata performing his father's rites and going with the townspeople to the Lord, the mine of joy; of Raghupati instructing them in many ways, after which Bharata took the sandals back to Ayodhya; of Bharata's manner of life, Indra's son's deed, and then the Lord's meeting with Atri.

He related the sanctifying of Dandaka forest and then friendship with Jatayu; the Lord's dwelling at Panchavati and the ending of all the sages' fear; Lakshmana's incomparable instruction and how Shurpanakha was disfigured; the killing of Khara and Dushana and how Ravana learned the entire secret; every detail of Ravana's conversation with Maricha; the abduction of illusory Sita and something of Shri Raghubira's grief of separation; how the Lord performed Jatayu's rites, killed Kabandha and gave Shabari the highest end; and, describing Raghubira's separation once more, how they reached the lake's shore.

He told how the monkey-king sent the monkeys racing in every direction to search for Sita; how they entered the cavern and afterward met Sampati; how the Wind's son heard the whole account and set out across the boundless ocean; how the monkey entered Lanka and reassured Sita; how he devastated the grove, warned Ravana, burned the city and crossed the ocean again; how all the monkeys returned to Raghuraya and reported Vaidehi's welfare; how Raghubira went with his army to the ocean's shore; how Vibhishana came and met him, and the story of subduing the ocean.

He related the many ways the demon hosts died and the battle of Raghupati and Ravana; Ravana's death, Mandodari's grief, Vibhishana's kingship and the gods' freedom from sorrow; Sita's reunion with Raghupati and the gods' praise with joined hands; then how the Lord, abode of grace, mounted Pushpaka with the monkeys and journeyed to Ayodhya. The crow sang in full how Rama returned to his own city, then told of Rama's consecration and, while describing the city, many principles of royal conduct. Bhushundi narrated the whole story that I have told you, Bhavani. Hearing all of Rama's story, the lord of birds spoke with supreme excitement in his heart.

‘Seeing the deeds so closely conform to human ways, a grave doubt arose in my heart. I now recognize that very delusion as a benefit: the treasure of grace has favoured me. Only one distressed by fierce heat knows the comfort of a tree's shade. Had intense delusion not overtaken me, dear one, how would I have met you? How could I have heard Hari's beautiful, many-sided and wondrous story as you have sung it? This is the doctrine of Veda, Agama and Purana, proclaimed without doubt by realized beings and sages: pure saints are met only by the one upon whom Rama gazes with grace. Through Rama's grace I gained your sight; through your favour all my doubts have gone.’

Kaka Bhushundi answered, his love for the lord of the sky no small thing: ‘Master, you are venerable to me in every way, a recipient of Raghunayaka's grace. You are untouched by doubt, delusion and Maya; Master, you have shown compassion to me. Using delusion as a pretext, Raghupati sent you here and bestowed greatness on me, lord of birds. You spoke of your own delusion, but that is no cause for wonder, Master. Narada, Shiva, Brahma, Sanaka and the other foremost self-realized sages—which of them has delusion not blinded at some time? Whom in the world has desire not made dance? Whom has craving not driven mad, and whose heart has anger not burned?’
